entries.title: Zero resistance: transport evidence and its limits
entries.summary: What a zero-resistance measurement establishes, which controls it needs, and why transport alone does not establish bulk superconductivity.

materialCases.temperatureNote: no equilibrium Tc assigned

entries.text:
Scope

A reported zero resistance is an operational result: the voltage is below the detection threshold for a specified current and contact geometry. The experiment establishes a bound on resistance rather than a mathematical proof that it is exactly zero. This article concerns electrical transport; magnetic expulsion and thermodynamic anomalies require separate measurements. The superconducting condensate provides the theoretical setting, but a microscopic model does not replace the experimental controls. 

Record resistance onset, midpoint and zero separately. An onset can identify a small superconducting region, whereas a connected path may determine the zero-resistance result. Neither number alone measures the superconducting volume fraction. Filaments, an interface or a second phase can dominate a four-terminal path even when most of the specimen remains normal. This distinction is central when comparing bulk crystals, films and high-pressure samples. 

 Mathematical assumptions

For a measured voltage resolution V{\mathrm{res}} and applied current I, an unresolved voltage implies the operational bound


R{\mathrm{meas}} < \frac{V{\mathrm{res}}}{|I|}.


This expression is a measurement definition, not a universal material law. It assumes a meaningful current path, stable contacts and a noise floor evaluated under the actual acquisition conditions. In a homogeneous specimen, converting resistance to resistivity further requires the sample dimensions. The ideal condensate response is a limiting statement about frequency, temperature, field and current; a finite experiment cannot take every limit simultaneously. 

 Experimental criteria

Use four-terminal measurements and show the raw resistance-versus-temperature or voltage-versus-current data. Report excitation current or current density, voltage threshold, field direction, sweep direction, contact arrangement and sample history. Repeat measurements at different currents to distinguish a robust transition from heating, a contact short or an instrument floor. For a claim of bulk superconductivity, seek independent magnetic or thermodynamic evidence. These are editorial evidence requirements, not a claim that one universal protocol fits every apparatus.

Halperin and Nelson developed a vortex-unbinding description of resistive behavior in dirty superconducting films, including fluctuation conductivity above an effective vortex-unbinding temperature and nonlinear resistivity below it. This is a theoretical treatment of a specified film regime, not a measurement of pairing symmetry. When applying it to data, this article requires independent checks of the model assumptions and sample conditions; a fit alone is not treated as a unique diagnosis. The publisher abstract supports this limited description; its full derivation has not yet been reviewed here. 

 Limits and disputes

Light-driven optical signatures must remain in a different evidence category from an equilibrium transport transition. Mitrano and colleagues reported a transient superconducting-like response in driven K3C60. The source chapter itself retains the ambiguity of assigning superconductivity from optics alone. Budden and colleagues investigated a longer-lived driven state with transport observations; those observations do not define an equilibrium zero-resistance critical temperature. This pilot does not promote either optical scale into a bulk temperature ranking.  

A persistent current can be complementary evidence, but its interpretation needs the loop geometry and decay time. A single low-resistance reading cannot supply those quantities. Likewise, magnetic-field suppression supports a superconducting interpretation without uniquely identifying the pairing interaction. 

 Discovery implications

Treat zero resistance as one part of an evidence chain. A useful candidate report specifies a measurable threshold, demonstrates repeatability and connects transport to other probes. Preserve negative controls and the possibility of a minority superconducting path. This approach makes a discovery claim more testable while keeping unresolved volume fraction, phase identity and mechanism explicitly open.  

 Related topics

Read  for magnetic tests,  for phase coherence, and  for normal-state transport inference.

entries.title: The Meissner effect and magnetic evidence
entries.summary: Distinguish equilibrium flux expulsion from shielding, then interpret penetration depth and magnetic volume estimates with their geometric assumptions.

materialCases.temperatureNote: not a temperature-record entry

entries.text:
Scope

The Meissner effect concerns the magnetic state selected on entering superconductivity. Meissner and Ochsenfeld's historical observation of flux expulsion is conceptually different from merely freezing the field already inside an ideal perfect conductor. Electrical transport and magnetic response therefore answer complementary questions. A sample may screen a changing field while retaining trapped vortices, so the cooling protocol must accompany a magnetization curve.  

Separate zero-field-cooled shielding, field-cooled magnetization and magnetic hysteresis. Strong pinning can make the field-cooled signal small even in a superconducting specimen. Conversely, a large shielding response cannot be read as an exact superconducting volume fraction without considering shape, connectivity and background subtraction. The magnetic inference belongs to the actual sample and protocol, not to a chemical formula in isolation. 

 Mathematical assumptions

The local, homogeneous London description gives


\nabla^2\mathbf B=\frac{\mathbf B}{\lambdaL^2}.


The penetration depth \lambdaL describes the decay of magnetic field in the stated limit. In a simple single-component convention, \lambdaL^{-2} is proportional to superfluid weight. Multiband, anisotropic or non-local electrodynamics requires a more careful response model; the same fitted depth need not represent the same microscopic density across those settings. 

For an approximately ellipsoidal specimen, the measured susceptibility is altered by a demagnetizing field. The correction depends on the field direction and shape. Quoting a shielding percentage without the underlying convention can produce values that look like a volume fraction but do not have that interpretation. The pilot therefore records the measurement criterion separately from any transition temperature. 

 Experimental criteria

Report specimen dimensions, orientation, applied field, cooling protocol, field history and background treatment. State whether the result is a shielding estimate, field-cooled expulsion, local magnetic response, penetration depth or sheet stiffness. Bulk claims benefit from consistency with transport and thermodynamic measurements rather than one isolated diamagnetic trace.

Low-temperature penetration-depth behavior constrains low-energy quasiparticles. Hardy and colleagues' YBCO microwave work is an important cuprate example, but extracting a gap structure still depends on impurity scattering, surface effects and the electrodynamic limit. A power law by itself does not uniquely identify an irreducible pairing representation. 

 Limits and disputes

Geometry, granularity and pinning can separate shielding from equilibrium flux expulsion. A small magnetic signal may reflect a small superconducting region, a difficult geometry or background uncertainty; these possibilities must be evaluated rather than silently choosing one. Likewise, magnetic screening alone does not identify a pairing mediator. 

Superfluid-density studies of overdoped La2-xSrxCuO4 constrain how the condensate evolves across a controlled sample series. Such correlations are useful but do not automatically determine a microscopic interaction. When comparing stiffness across two- and three-dimensional systems, retain thickness and the electromagnetic normalization. A geometric contribution cannot be obtained merely by relabeling a measured total stiffness. 

 Discovery implications

A persuasive magnetic evidence package documents what field is excluded, which part is trapped and how the susceptibility was corrected. Pair transport and magnetic probes on comparable samples. For thin films, explicitly report whether the inferred quantity is a sheet response or a bulk penetration depth. These distinctions support reproducibility without turning an inversion model into an unqualified material property.  

 Related topics

Compare , , and .

entries.title: Specific heat: the jump, entropy balance and bulk evidence
entries.summary: Read a thermodynamic anomaly with its background, normalization and transition criterion. The BCS jump is a model benchmark, not a universal verdict.
entries.text:
Scope

Heat capacity probes the change of entropy with temperature. A superconducting anomaly can therefore provide a bulk thermodynamic check that complements resistance and magnetic screening. A peak alone does not identify its cause: magnetic, structural and charge-order transitions can also produce anomalies. This article separates an ideal electronic heat-capacity jump from the measured total signal and from an empirical trend across different samples.

Use C on a declared basis: per mole, per unit mass, per volume or for the entire sample. The normalization of the normal-state electronic coefficient \gamman must match. Experiments often measure Cp, while a simple electronic model evaluates heat capacity with a fixed spectrum and volume. Their difference may be small for an appropriate low-temperature solid, but that approximation should be justified when quantitative precision matters.

 Mathematical assumptions

For an isotropic single-band weak-coupling BCS model with a smooth density of states, define the electronic jump on cooling as \Delta Ce=C{es}(Tc^-)-C{en}(Tc^+). Its limiting value is


\frac{\Delta Ce}{\gammanTc}=\frac{12}{7\zeta(3)}\simeq1.426.


Here C{en}=\gammanT in the assumed low-temperature normal state. The number is a model benchmark, not a threshold that every superconductor must pass. Johnston gives the limiting expression in Eq. (22) of the cited author manuscript. 

Entropy follows from dS=C\,dT/T under the specified thermodynamic constraints. For a continuous transition with equal extrapolated zero-temperature entropies in the compared phases,


Ss(Tc)-Sn(Tc)=\int0^{Tc}\frac{Cs(T)-Cn(T)}{T}\,dT=0.


The normal curve below Tc is a defined reference, not a directly accessible zero-field equilibrium phase. Background subtraction and low-temperature extrapolation therefore affect the test. A first-order transition has latent heat and requires a different treatment. Do not force this continuous-transition construction onto such a dataset.

An independent numerical check for this entry solved the constant-density-of-states gap equation, integrated the quasiparticle entropy and differentiated it near Tc. The normalized jump approaches 1.426 as the cutoff and numerical step are controlled; the normalized entropy reaches the normal-state value at the transition. This checks the stated model and conventions, not a material dataset. The entropy and heat-capacity relations are consistent with the selected manuscript equations. 

 Experimental criteria

Start from the measured heat capacity and report addenda, sample mass and calibration uncertainty. A fit such as Cn/T=\gamman+\beta T^2 assumes a linear electronic term and a low-temperature lattice contribution. It can fail if extra excitations or nearby transitions matter. State the temperature interval and uncertainty of the background, and show how another reasonable background changes the inferred anomaly.

A field used to suppress superconductivity is not automatically a perfect normal-state reference. Check whether it reaches the normal state over the relevant range and whether it changes magnetic or other contributions. Use the same units and sample basis in the field and zero-field curves. Show transition width, the chosen thermodynamic Tc and the entropy comparison, rather than only a peak height.

Compare with resistance and screening on the same or demonstrably comparable specimen. A consistent anomaly with the expected field response strengthens the case for bulk superconductivity. Failure to resolve an anomaly may instead reflect sensitivity, sample size, a small superconducting fraction or an incorrect baseline. It leaves thermodynamic confirmation incomplete; it does not by itself establish absence of superconductivity. These are reporting and interpretation criteria from the pinned chapter, not independently verified measurements.

 Limits and disputes

The phenomenological alpha model retains the BCS normalized gap shape while varying \alpha=\Delta(0)/(kBTc) in the thermodynamic calculation. Padamsee and colleagues describe its quasiparticle construction in their abstract. A successful fit is not a microscopic derivation of the interaction. 

Within that model the jump scales as 1.426(\alpha/\alpha{\rm BCS})^2. This does not mean that the entire entropy or heat-capacity curve can simply be multiplied by that factor: the occupation functions also change. Gap anisotropy or multiple coupled bands can alter the normalized jump. Multiple bands do not necessarily broaden a single sharp transition; disorder, phase mixtures and a distribution of local transition temperatures are separate issues. 

Bud'ko, Ni and Canfield report an empirical relation \Delta Cp/Tc\propto Tc^2 for their substituted Ba122 series together with specified literature samples. Equivalently, the jump itself scales as Tc^3 within that comparison. This is a dataset-dependent observation, not a fundamental law or a stand-alone proof of a pairing mechanism. The current check covers the publisher abstract, not a reanalysis of the data. 

 Discovery implications

Use an anomaly to constrain a proposed state together with independent probes. Ask which part of the temperature dependence is reliable, how much of the sample participates, and whether competing backgrounds could produce the same result. Preserve disagreement between probes and the uncertainty in extrapolated quantities.

A useful next experiment resolves a specific ambiguity: a field-dependent background, an uncertain phase fraction, a residual low-temperature term or an alternative gap distribution. Comparing a single normalized jump to 1.426 cannot uniquely select gap symmetry, coupling strength or a mediator. These are model-discrimination questions, not new experimental findings.

 Related topics

Connect heat capacity to , , , , and .

entries.title: Isotope effect: mass response and pairing constraints
entries.summary: Separate partial and total isotope coefficients, preserve experimental criteria, and test the assumptions behind the one-half benchmark.

materialCases.sample: boron-10 sample, solid piece from reacted pellet
materialCases.temperatureNote: Magnetic onset in 25 G; not zero resistance or a zero-field thermodynamic Tc
materialCases.probe: SQUID magnetization, warming after zero-field cooling; 2% of low-temperature diamagnetic signal

materialCases.sample: boron-11 sample, solid piece from reacted pellet
materialCases.temperatureNote: Magnetic onset in 25 G; not zero resistance or a zero-field thermodynamic Tc
materialCases.probe: SQUID magnetization, warming after zero-field cooling; 2% of low-temperature diamagnetic signal

entries.text:
Scope

Isotope substitution changes nuclear mass while keeping the element the same. The resulting response of a transition temperature can constrain lattice involvement, provided the compared samples have controlled chemistry and structure. It does not, by itself, identify the complete pairing interaction. This entry distinguishes a mass derivative, a finite comparison between samples and a microscopic explanation.

The classic mercury reports by Maxwell and Reynolds and colleagues, and Fröhlich's early theory paper, are historical starting points. Their bibliographic identities are checked here; their original experimental curves and derivations are not. No mercury exponent is extracted from those metadata records.   

 Mathematical assumptions

For element i, with other masses and specified sample conditions held fixed, define

\alphai=-\frac{\partial\ln Tc}{\partial\ln Mi},\qquad \widehat\alphai=-\frac{\ln(T{c,2}/T{c,1})}{\ln(M{i,2}/M{i,1})}.

The finite estimate averages a slope over the chosen interval; it equals the local derivative only for an appropriate limiting interval or a power law. Use the mean mass implied by measured isotope abundances, not automatically an integer isotope label. A partial coefficient is not the total \alpha{\rm tot}=\sumi\alphai. This sum describes a common logarithmic scaling of all component masses under the same constraints. 

For a harmonic mode with fixed force constant, \omega\propto M^{-1/2}. If the transition scale is proportional to that frequency and all dimensionless interaction parameters remain mass independent, differentiation gives \alpha=1/2. The fixed-parameter condition is essential. A measured deviation challenges that restricted model, not every possible electron–phonon theory. 

An illustrative two-mass optical oscillator makes the distinction concrete. If \omega^2=K(1/M1+1/M2) and Tc\propto\omega, direct differentiation gives

\alpha1=\frac{M2}{2(M1+M2)},\qquad \alpha2=\frac{M1}{2(M1+M2)},\qquad \alpha1+\alpha2=\frac12.

Each partial coefficient can be below one half even in this harmonic construction. These equations are a local illustrative derivation, checked against numerical mass derivatives; they are not a fit to MgB2 or a microscopic pairing calculation.

For uncertainty propagation let N=\ln(T{c,2}/T{c,1}) and D=\ln(M{i,2}/M{i,1}). First-order propagation for \widehat\alpha=-N/D gives

\sigma\alpha^2\simeq\frac{\operatorname{Var}(N)}{D^2}+\frac{N^2\operatorname{Var}(D)}{D^4}-\frac{2N\operatorname{Cov}(N,D)}{D^3}.

This linear approximation requires small uncertainties relative to the resolved mass interval. Shared calibration errors can be correlated; treating all temperatures as independent can misstate the uncertainty. The analytic gradient was checked against finite differences. Those arithmetic checks do not establish experimental precision.

 Experimental criteria

Bud'ko and colleagues report MgB2 isotope samples with magnetic onsets at 40.2 K for boron-10 and 39.2 K for boron-11. They use 25 G, warming after zero-field cooling, and a 2% onset of the low-temperature diamagnetic signal. Heat capacity also shows the shift. Their reported boron coefficient is 0.26\pm0.03, a partial coefficient. Using nominal masses 10 and 11 gives about 0.264 from the stated temperatures; this only checks arithmetic, not enrichment or their error estimate. 

A separate study by Hinks, Claus and Jorgensen measures both components. Its author manuscript reports partial coefficients of 0.30(1) for boron and 0.02(1) for magnesium, with total 0.32(1). Its magnetic protocol uses 1 G and compares extrapolated onset with a 10% criterion. These values belong to that study and must not be assembled from unrelated samples or criteria. The authors explicitly discuss possible impurity effects in their magnesium comparison. 

For a new comparison, report enrichment, composition, structure, defects, preparation history and the exact temperature criterion. Characterize spectral frequency shifts where feasible. Back-exchange can test reversibility, but annealing itself may change the specimen. Repeat controls and uncertainty estimates are needed before assigning a shift exclusively to mass. These are editorial reporting recommendations, not claims that every cited study performed every control.

 Limits and disputes

A small response for one element does not exclude its contribution to a coupled vibrational system. Conversely, a nonzero response does not reconstruct the full electron–phonon spectral function or uniquely determine a mediator. Mass-dependent interactions, anharmonicity and structural changes require explicit models; the sign or size alone cannot settle them. The cited Hinks manuscript discusses alternatives to its own interaction-parameter interpretation. 

Do not merge resistive onset, zero resistance, magnetic screening and a calorimetric transition into one unqualified temperature. The material records below preserve the magnetic criterion actually checked. Pressure and equilibrium classifications not established in the selected passages remain unknown. Comparing isotope coefficients from different studies also requires their sample preparation and systematic uncertainties.

 Discovery implications

Ask which controlled observation would separate a direct mass dependence from a changed sample. Joint measurements of structure, composition, vibrational spectra and independent superconducting probes can narrow the interpretation. Preserve null results and disagreements rather than treating the isotope exponent as a pass/fail label.

A quantitative theory should predict the response of the same observable under the same substitution and constraints. Agreement with one coefficient is a consistency check; a credible explanation must also confront the remaining measurements. These are model-discrimination criteria, not a new material discovery.

 Related topics

Read the , , , , and  alongside an isotope comparison.

entries.title: Superconducting gap: magnitude, nodes and phase
entries.summary: Read gap measurements with their probe and model. Distinguish an excitation scale from evidence for nodes, relative sign or bulk superconductivity.
entries.text:
Scope

A superconducting gap is an energy scale in a specified excitation spectrum. Its magnitude, momentum dependence and relative phase answer different questions. A suppression of spectral weight is not automatically a superconducting gap, and a fitted gap does not automatically define the temperature of bulk superconductivity. This entry organizes observations and model assumptions rather than ranking materials by a single gap ratio.

Specify whether \Delta denotes an order-parameter amplitude, a quasiparticle excitation threshold or a parameter extracted from a broadened spectrum. The relation between these quantities depends on the model. Keep the measured signal, the fit and the inferred state separate; otherwise apparently similar numbers can describe different observables.

 Mathematical assumptions

For a clean, isotropic, single-band weak-coupling BCS model, the quasiparticle spectrum and zero-temperature limiting ratio are

E{\mathbf k}=\sqrt{\xi{\mathbf k}^{\,2}+|\Delta|^2},\qquad \frac{2\Delta0}{kBTc}=2\pi e^{-\gammaE}\simeq3.528.

Here \xi{\mathbf k} is measured from the chemical potential and \gammaE is Euler's constant. The existing BCS entry checks the gap equation and numerical limit. The ratio is not a universal threshold for identifying superconductivity or an interaction. Strong coupling and anisotropy require their own treatment; Carbotte's review abstract describes deviations from simple BCS results without supplying a universal correction.  

With a constant normal density of states Nn and the same spin convention in numerator and denominator, the ideal normalized density of states at positive excitation energy is

\frac{Ns(E)}{Nn}=\begin{cases}0,&0\le E<|\Delta|,\\ E/\sqrt{E^2-|\Delta|^2},&E>|\Delta|.\end{cases}

The factor above the edge follows from the change of variable E=\sqrt{\xi^2+|\Delta|^2} with the usual Bogoliubov spectral weights. The ideal edge is singular but integrable. A local numerical check integrates it up to a finite energy and recovers the corresponding normal-state \xi interval. The check assumes no lifetime broadening, gap anisotropy or experimental convolution. 

In this magnitude-only model, replacing a gap by its negative leaves the excitation energies unchanged. Likewise, independently summing two uncoupled spectral contributions cannot recover their relative sign. This is a limited counterexample to inferring phase from a gap magnitude; it does not say that every interference-sensitive spectrum is phase blind.

 Experimental criteria

Use the following as a reporting map adapted from the pinned chapter. Each interpretation needs the stated model and a sample-specific source; these rows do not certify any material dataset.

| Probe | Recorded quantity | What must be controlled |
|---|---|---|
| Tunneling or STS | Differential conductance versus bias | Tip and sample spectra, thermal/instrumental broadening, matrix elements and surface variation |
| ARPES | Momentum-resolved photoemission intensity | Occupation, resolution, matrix elements and surface state; a leading edge is not automatically a gap amplitude |
| Optical or THz spectroscopy | Frequency-dependent electrodynamic response | Scattering, multiple bands and the model linking absorption to an excitation threshold |
| Heat capacity | Entropy and bulk excitation contribution | Lattice/magnetic backgrounds and normalization; no direct phase measurement |
| Penetration depth or thermal transport | Low-energy electromagnetic or heat response | Disorder, nonlocality, background and multiple excitation channels |
| Andreev or point-contact spectroscopy | Interface current and conductance | Barrier transparency, heating, contact regime and channel mixing |

A tunnel conductance resembles the sample density of states only with suitable assumptions about the counterelectrode and tunneling matrix element, and after accounting for the thermal convolution. Do not identify every conductance peak with \Delta. Photoemission and thermodynamic measurements constrain different aspects of the state; the selected review discusses why magnitude-sensitive probes alone do not measure the relative phase. 

Hardy and colleagues report a strong linear term in the penetration-depth change of YBa2Cu3O6.95 single crystals over approximately 3–25 K using a 900 MHz resonator. This is evidence relevant to low-energy excitations under their sample conditions, not a direct measurement of gap phase. The present check covers the publisher abstract. 

By contrast, Tsuei and Kirtley use scanning SQUID measurements of NCCO/PCCO tricrystals to test phase-sensitive predictions. Their designed frustrated geometry produces a half-flux signal, while two unfrustrated NCCO geometries serve as controls. The inference depends on junction geometry and the associated model, not merely on observing a spectral dip. Selected author-manuscript passages and the control description were checked; the image fits were not independently reproduced. 

 Limits and disputes

Nodes, relative sign and topology are distinct. A low-temperature power law can constrain low-energy excitations without uniquely selecting a pairing representation. A fully open gap on each Fermi-surface sheet can coexist with a relative sign change between sheets. Disorder and sample inhomogeneity must be considered before translating a temperature dependence into a symmetry assignment. 

A zero-bias feature alone is not a unique topology test. Identify its field, temperature, position and junction dependence, then compare explicit alternative models. Likewise, a spectroscopic gap-closing temperature must not silently replace a resistive or thermodynamic Tc in a gap ratio. These are inference and reporting limits, not a claim that one alternative explains every observed feature.

Choi and colleagues' MgB2 result is an anisotropic Eliashberg calculation of distinct band-dependent gap scales. Treat those calculated gaps as theory and compare them with separately identified measurements. The pinned chapter's DOI was mismatched; the correct source is nature00898. That correction does not validate a universal multiband gap ratio or independently reproduce the calculation. 

 Discovery implications

Record the specimen, pressure or strain, temperature criterion, spectral resolution, fit model and uncertainty together. Compare probes on the same or demonstrably comparable specimens. A disagreement can expose a surface effect, background assumption or a second energy scale; it should remain visible until tested.

A useful next measurement distinguishes competing interpretations. Establish which observation would separate a change of magnitude from a change of phase, and which control would rule out a contact artifact or another ordered state. Gap measurements constrain models; they do not replace a complete evidence chain for superconductivity.

 Related topics

Connect to , , , , , and .

entries.title: Critical fields: thermodynamic, orbital and Pauli scales
entries.summary: Distinguish Hc, Hc1 and Hc2, compare orbital and spin limits, and keep experimental field criteria attached to their conditions.
entries.text:
Scope

A critical field needs a physical definition. The thermodynamic field Hc represents the zero-field condensation-energy density, fn-fs=\mu0Hc^2/2. This energy scale exists for both type-I and type-II superconductors; it is not generally the field at which a type-II sample becomes normal. In the ideal bulk type-II description, H{c1} marks the equilibrium onset of the mixed state and H{c2} its upper boundary. The vortex construction distinguishes those boundaries from one thermodynamic energy scale. 

Here H is magnetic field strength in amperes per metre, while B and \mu0H are expressed in tesla. Inside matter, B=\mu0(H+M); replacing B by \mu0H requires a stated magnetization approximation. An applied-field value, an internal field and a flux density must not silently share the same symbol. The formulas below use SI conventions, rather than copying Gaussian-unit factors from historical papers.

 Mathematical assumptions

For a bulk, isotropic, single-component Ginzburg–Landau model near Tc, neglecting paramagnetic pair breaking, linearization gives the orbital result


B{c2}^{\mathrm{orb}}=\frac{\Phi0}{2\pi\xi^2},\qquad
\Phi0=\frac{h}{2e},\qquad
\kappa=\frac{\lambda}{\xi}.


The usual \mu0H{c2}^{\mathrm{orb}} notation uses B\simeq\mu0H near this continuous boundary when normal-state magnetic response is negligible. In the same model, H{c2}^{\mathrm{orb}}=\sqrt{2}\kappa Hc. The GL coherence length \xi and penetration depth \lambda are evaluated at the same temperature. They are not interchangeable with every microscopic pair-size or fitted length. The isotropic GL type-II boundary is \kappa=1/\sqrt{2}. 

A useful independent check follows from the linearized kinetic operator: the lowest Landau-level energy of a pair with charge magnitude 2e is \hbar(2e)B/(2m^\ast). Equating it to |\alpha|, with \xi^2=\hbar^2/(2m^\ast|\alpha|), gives the flux-over-area expression above. This is a model derivation, not a measured field or an all-temperature interpolation.

For a separate, purely paramagnetic comparison at zero temperature, take an isotropic weak-coupling singlet with g=2, negligible spin susceptibility in the paired state, no orbital cost and no competing modulated state. Equating its condensation energy to the normal-state polarization-energy gain gives


BP=\frac{\Delta0}{\sqrt{2}\muB},\qquad
\frac{BP}{Tc}=\frac{\pi e^{-\gamma}kB}{\sqrt{2}\muB}
\simeq 1.86\;\mathrm{T\,K^{-1}}.


This is the Clogston–Chandrasekhar reference scale. The commonly quoted 1.84\;\mathrm{T\,K^{-1}} uses rounded weak-coupling gap constants; neither coefficient is an exact universal experimental bound. The numerical value here uses the same modern weak-coupling gap convention as the BCS entry. The energy comparison is supported by the cited perspective; the original Clogston paper's identity is checked, but its full text was not available in this review.   

 Experimental criteria

Report the probe and the rule used to locate a field line. Resistance onset, a stated percentage of the normal-state resistance and a voltage-resolution-limited zero need not coincide. Neither a magnetic irreversibility line nor a first flux-entry signal should automatically be renamed H{c2} or equilibrium H{c1}. Demagnetizing geometry, surface barriers, vortex motion, pinning and inhomogeneous current paths can affect the observed signal.

Record temperature, field orientation and angular uncertainty, sample geometry, pressure where relevant, current density, sweep direction and rate, and the normal-state baseline. Compare transport with an appropriate bulk thermodynamic or magnetic measurement on comparable specimens. Preserve hysteresis and transition widths instead of choosing the most favorable boundary. These are measurement-reporting requirements from the pinned chapter, not a claim that each possible artifact is present in a particular sample.

 Limits and disputes

Werthamer–Helfand–Hohenberg theory treats orbital and spin effects within a specified microscopic approximation, including spin–orbit impurity scattering. Its publisher abstract explicitly notes that such scattering counteracts paramagnetic limiting. A fitted WHH curve therefore needs its dirty-limit, spin and scattering assumptions; merely naming the fit does not establish them. This entry's WHH check is abstract-scoped. 

Multiband structure also changes extrapolation. Gurevich's dirty two-gap model allows H{c2}(T) shapes controlled by different intraband diffusivities, including deviations from the one-gap slope estimate near Tc. That calculation is a counterexample to treating a one-band extrapolation coefficient as universal. It does not validate an arbitrary multiband fit or supply a field value for an unmeasured sample. 

Exceeding the simple Pauli estimate does not uniquely identify triplet pairing. The spin response and spin–orbit energy scales may differ from the assumed reference model; the cited Ising-superconductivity perspective discusses a concrete route to a strongly anisotropic paramagnetic response. Orbital and spin limitations must be treated together when both matter. No material-specific critical-field record or pairing assignment is introduced here. 

 Discovery implications

Use a field measurement to discriminate between declared models. First decide whether the observation concerns an equilibrium boundary, vortex dynamics or a transport threshold. Then test orientation and temperature dependence over a range where the model applies. Retain the fitting window, parameter uncertainty and alternative descriptions, particularly when extrapolating far below the measured temperatures.

A high critical field may motivate further study, but a useful discovery argument identifies which assumption failed and which new observable could distinguish the remaining explanations. Material comparisons should keep pressure, field direction and criterion attached to each value. A large fitted field alone establishes neither a microscopic pairing mediator nor topology. This is an editorial evaluation protocol; it is not a newly verified experimental result.

 Related topics

Read about , , , and .

entries.title: Critical current: criteria, geometry and pinning
entries.summary: Compare transport, magnetization and depairing limits with their field, time scale and area convention. Preserve measurement conditions before comparing conductor performance.
entries.text:
Scope

Critical current is a limit defined for a specimen, measurement protocol and operating conditions. Transport measurements use a voltage or electric-field criterion; magnetization measurements infer a current through a model; the depairing current describes loss of stability of a superconducting state within a specified theory. These quantities must not share an unlabeled performance ranking.

Blatter and colleagues explicitly distinguish depinning and depairing current densities in their review abstract. Pinning, thermal fluctuations and vortex motion affect practical current transport. A measured threshold can instead be limited by weak connections or heating; its mechanism requires evidence beyond the value of the current itself. 

 Mathematical assumptions

For voltage taps separated by length L, define the mean longitudinal electric-field criterion Ec=Vc/L. Using the same measured Ic, distinguish the nominal superconducting cross-section As from the entire conductor area At:

Jc=\frac{Ic}{As},\qquad Je=\frac{Ic}{At}=fJc,\qquad f=\frac{As}{At}.

Here Je is an engineering current density for the stated whole-conductor area. Nominal superconducting area does not resolve nonuniform current paths or pores. A different definition of non-copper area, filament area or cable area requires a different label. These identities compare area conventions; they do not correct a damaged conductor or infer intrinsic microscopic current density.

A simple sensitivity calculation illustrates why the criterion matters. If a measured interval is modeled by E=E0(J/J0)^n with positive constant n, changing the criterion by a factor r changes the inferred current by r^{1/n}. For n=20, a tenfold criterion change gives a factor of about 1.122. This is an illustrative power-law calculation, not a measured exponent or a universal transport law.

The magnetic force density is the vector product \mathbf F=\mathbf J\times\mathbf B. For current perpendicular to the induction, its magnitude at the threshold becomes Fp=JcB if a static pinning-force balance is the applicable model. In SI units this is N/m³; resistive heating instead has power density \mathbf E\cdot\mathbf J in W/m³. A parallel configuration has no force from this cross product. Replacing B by \mu0H requires an additional approximation, especially near self-field conditions.

For an explicit geometry check, take an infinite slab of full thickness 2a, field parallel to its faces, constant Jc and fully developed opposite critical-state branches. Neglect demagnetization, reversible magnetization and creep. Ampere's law gives |dB/dx|=\mu0Jc. With x measured across the thickness, the ideal branch profiles are B\pm(x)=\mu0[Ha\pm Jc(a-|x|)]. Their spatial averages give

M\pm=\pm\frac{Jca}{2},\qquad \Delta M=M+-M-=Jca,\qquad Jc=\frac{\Delta M}{a}.

\Delta M is the full vertical loop width in A/m; a is the half-thickness in metres. Numerically integrating these stated profiles verifies the factor and dimensions. This is a local derivation under ideal assumptions, not a reanalysis of Bean's original data. Bean's 1962 paper is the historical source; its full text was not available in this check. Do not transfer this slab expression to arbitrary films, cylinders, partial penetration or field-dependent Jc. 

 Experimental criteria

Keep enough information to reconstruct both the measured threshold and the conversion to a current density. The following is an editorial reporting guide, not a table of certified material records.

| Measurement | Record with the result | Interpretation boundary |
|---|---|---|
| Transport | Temperature, field magnitude and orientation, voltage-tap spacing, electric-field criterion, current ramp or pulse duration, duty cycle, area convention | Contact heating, current sharing and voltage offsets can change the inferred threshold |
| Magnetization | Magnetic moment, volume, dimensions, field history, sweep rate, elapsed time and background subtraction | Conversion to current requires a geometry and critical-state model |
| Conductor or cable | Superconducting fraction, whole-conductor area, length, strain and thermal stabilization | Layer current density and engineering current density answer different questions |
| Depairing model | Model, temperature regime, geometry and stability assumptions | A calculated instability is not automatically the measured transport limit |

MacManus-Driscoll and colleagues studied YBCO films grown with BaZrO3 added to the target. Their selected manuscript passages report improved in-field transport at 75.5 K, despite lower transition temperature or self-field current in some samples. The rotated field remained perpendicular to current. This comparison illustrates distinct performance measures, not proof of a different pairing mechanism. No electric-field criterion was extracted here, so no numerical current record is tabulated. 

Larbalestier and colleagues' 2014 paper is a primary Bi-2212 round-wire study, not a general engineering review. Its earlier author manuscript distinguishes whole-conductor Je from superconducting-area Jc and compares short specimens with a demonstration coil. This entry uses that distinction without importing a cross-family ranking; the final published dataset and all measurement criteria were not independently re-extracted. 

 Limits and disputes

An irreversible magnetic response and the upper critical field are different observables. A loss of measurable hysteresis or a transport threshold need not locate the destruction of superconductivity. Report the criterion, time scale and field history rather than silently equating an irreversibility line with H{c2}. Thermally activated creep is one reason different observation times can yield different apparent current limits. 

A fitted pinning-curve exponent or angular peak does not uniquely identify a defect. Compare microscopy, processing controls and temperature/angle dependence. In the checked YBCO manuscript, the detailed composition of the small second-phase particles is not conclusively established; describing every particle as chemically proven BaZrO3 would overstate the evidence. 

 Discovery implications

Separate a better transport path, stronger pinning, a larger superconducting fraction and a higher depairing limit as distinct hypotheses. Compare controlled specimens under matched conditions before assigning an improvement to a microscopic mechanism. A gain in current-carrying performance does not by itself demonstrate higher Tc, a new pairing interaction or a new superconducting phase.

Preserve the measured signal, uncertainty and analysis conventions together. If the voltage criterion, geometry or thermal history is unavailable, retain that gap in the record. A useful follow-up is the measurement that discriminates between the competing limits, rather than another unsupported performance ranking.

entries.title: BCS theory: the weak-coupling baseline
entries.summary: Cooper pairing, the gap equation and the 3.528 gap ratio, with the assumptions that make these useful model benchmarks rather than universal material rules.
entries.text:
Scope

BCS theory provides a microscopic pairing framework and a useful weak-coupling reference point. This article concerns its equilibrium, single-band, isotropic implementation with a smooth density of states and an effective attraction near the Fermi surface. Those assumptions define a model, not a classification of every superconductor. Agreement with one numerical ratio does not uniquely identify a pairing interaction. 

The Cooper problem asks what happens when two electrons interact above an otherwise inert, filled Fermi sea. In the idealized attractive-shell model, a bound pair exists below the two-particle continuum for arbitrarily weak net attraction. The filled sea and its excluded states are essential to this result. It is not a claim that every attractive potential binds two isolated electrons in vacuum, nor is the two-electron calculation alone a construction of the finite-density superconducting state. 

 Mathematical assumptions

Write the attractive matrix element as -V, with V>0. Let N(0) count states of one spin per unit energy, using the same volume normalization as V, so \lambda=N(0)V is dimensionless. The energy cutoff is Ec=\hbar\omegac, where \omegac is an angular frequency. With \xi measured relative to the chemical potential, the excitation spectrum and gap equation are


E(\xi)=\sqrt{\xi^2+|\Delta|^2},



1=\lambda\int0^{Ec}\frac{\tanh[E(\xi)/(2kBT)]}{E(\xi)}\,d\xi.


The positive-energy integral already accounts for the symmetric negative-energy interval in the momentum-sum formulation. Inserting a two-spin density of states without changing the prefactor doubles the effective coupling. At zero temperature this model gives \Delta0=Ec/\sinh(1/\lambda). For \lambda\ll1, the usual limiting forms are


kBTc\simeq\frac{2e^\gamma}{\pi}Ec e^{-1/\lambda},



\frac{2\Delta0}{kBTc}\simeq2\pi e^{-\gamma}\simeq3.528.


Here \gamma is the Euler–Mascheroni constant; 2e^\gamma/\pi\simeq1.134. These are model results, not a measured transition temperature. We use modern \Delta notation for the single-quasiparticle threshold; creating two quasiparticles costs at least 2\Delta in this idealized spectrum. The original paper used different notation and rounded numerical estimates. 

 Experimental criteria

A useful comparison needs a gap measurement and a separately specified superconducting transition criterion on a comparable sample. Report whether the measured quantity is a single-particle threshold, a pair-breaking energy or a fitted spectral parameter. State temperature, magnetic field, sample composition and uncertainty before calculating a gap ratio. A peak separation must not silently be substituted for \Delta0.

Then compare more than one observable: the temperature evolution of the gap, electronic thermodynamics and magnetic response constrain different aspects of the state. Distinguish a consistency test of the isotropic weak-coupling model from evidence for a particular microscopic mediator. No sample-specific Tc or gap value is added to the material-comparison catalogue by this theoretical article. 

 Limits and disputes

The general pairing construction should not be equated with a universal weak-coupling phonon mechanism. A frequency-dependent interaction, several coupled bands, an anisotropic gap or a rapidly varying density of states requires a more suitable equation. Phase fluctuations can also separate a pairing scale from the temperature at which long-range or quasi-long-range coherence develops. The simple gap equation above does not calculate that fluctuation problem.

The familiar isotope exponent -d\ln Tc/d\ln M=1/2 follows only if the cutoff has harmonic mass scaling and the remaining effective parameters are mass-independent. Changes in structure or coupling invalidate that inference. Likewise, a nonstandard gap ratio can motivate tests of stronger coupling or anisotropy; it does not, by itself, prove a named alternative mechanism. These applicability cautions follow the scope of the pinned B1 source chapter and are not new experimental findings. 

 Discovery implications

Use BCS as a controlled baseline: define the band model, interaction window and normalization before fitting. Check that the inferred scales fit within the regime assumed by the calculation, rather than extrapolating an exponential formula into a flat-band or low-density regime. Compare alternative explanations using measurements that distinguish them. In particular, finding a Cooper instability is a starting point for a many-body theory, not the final demonstration of a material's phase coherence or pairing mediator. 

A productive research record should retain which assumption failed, which observation exposed the failure and which additional measurement could decide between the remaining models. This is editorial guidance for using the baseline, not a claim of an experimentally established route to higher Tc.

 Related topics
